The European Ombudsman investigates complaints about maladministration in the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the European Union. Maladministration is understood broadly: it covers not only unlawful acts but also unfairness, unjustified delays, refusal to provide information and failure to reply. The office was created by the Maastricht Treaty, and the first Ombudsman took up duties in 1995; the post-holder is elected by the European Parliament after each European election, for a renewable term matching the Parliament's.

Any citizen or resident of the EU, as well as any company, association or other body with a registered office in a Member State, may lodge a complaint, normally within two years of becoming aware of the problem. The complainant must first have tried to resolve the matter with the institution concerned. Complaints about national, regional or local authorities fall outside the remit, even when those authorities are implementing EU law, and the Court of Justice acting in its judicial role cannot be investigated either.

The Ombudsman cannot issue binding decisions. Instead, the office may propose a solution, make recommendations and, if an institution does not respond satisfactorily, submit a special report to the Parliament. In practice, much of its influence comes from the publicity that such findings attract.
statement: If an institution ignores a recommendation, the Ombudsman refers the case to the Court of Justice.
currentNote: Not supported. The text names a special report to the Parliament as the next step; it never mentions a referral to the Court of Justice.

Adopted in 2019, the EU Directive on single-use plastics targets the ten single-use plastic items most often found on European beaches, together with fishing gear. The measures differ according to whether sustainable alternatives exist. Where alternatives are readily available and affordable, products such as plastic cutlery, plates, straws, cotton bud sticks and expanded polystyrene food containers were banned from the EU market from July 2021.

For products without such alternatives, including tobacco filters and wet wipes, the Directive relies on other tools. Member States must reduce the consumption of plastic food containers and drinks cups, and producers of the products concerned must contribute to the costs of waste management and of cleaning up litter under 'extended producer responsibility' schemes. Certain products must also carry a label informing consumers about the plastic they contain and the appropriate way to dispose of them.

Plastic beverage bottles are subject to specific targets: they must contain at least 25% recycled plastic by 2025 for PET bottles and 30% by 2030 for all such bottles, and Member States must collect 77% of them separately by 2025 and 90% by 2029. Since July 2024, caps and lids have had to remain attached to bottles during use.
statement: Wherever an alternative to a plastic product exists, the plastic version has been banned, whatever the price.
currentNote: False. Bans apply where alternatives are 'readily available and affordable', so price does matter.

Research on learning consistently finds that retrieval practice, which means actively recalling information, for instance by testing oneself, leads to better long-term retention than simply rereading material. The benefit appears even when the test is not marked and no feedback is given, although feedback increases it further. Curiously, learners often feel less confident after retrieval practice than after rereading, because recalling information is effortful and exposes gaps, and many therefore prefer the less effective method.

A related finding concerns timing. Spreading study sessions over days or weeks, known as spaced practice, tends to produce more durable learning than concentrating the same amount of study into one session. 'Cramming' can improve performance in a test taken shortly afterwards, but the material is forgotten more quickly. The best gap between sessions seems to depend on how long the information needs to be remembered.

Some researchers also recommend 'interleaving', which means mixing different types of problem within a session instead of practising one type at a time. Interleaving feels harder and initially produces more errors, but in several studies it improved learners' ability to recognise which method a new problem requires.
statement: Spaced practice works best when the study sessions are held exactly one week apart.
currentNote: False. The best gap 'seems to depend' on how long the material must be remembered; no fixed interval is given.

The European Capital of Culture initiative was launched in 1985 on the suggestion of Greek culture minister Melina Mercouri, and Athens was the first city to hold the title. Today, two cities in different EU Member States hold it each year, and every third year a third city from a candidate country, a potential candidate or a member of the European Free Trade Association that belongs to the European Economic Area is also designated.

Cities are not simply appointed. They compete in national selection rounds, a panel of independent experts recommends the winners, and the cities are formally designated four years before the title year, after which their preparations are monitored. The title itself comes with only a modest EU prize, named after Melina Mercouri, which is paid if the city fulfils its commitments; most of the funding comes from national, regional and local budgets and from private sponsors.

Evaluations suggest that the title can boost tourism and urban regeneration, as in Glasgow in 1990 and Lille in 2004, but that the benefits are uneven: some cities struggled to maintain cultural activity once the year was over, and others were criticised for spending heavily on buildings rather than on local cultural participation.
statement: Holding the title guarantees lasting economic benefits for the city that is chosen.
currentNote: False. The text says the benefits are 'uneven' and that some cities 'struggled to maintain cultural activity once the year was over', so nothing lasting is guaranteed.

Under EU rules on air passenger rights, travellers may be entitled to fixed compensation of €250, €400 or €600, depending on the distance of the flight, if their flight is cancelled less than 14 days before departure. The rules themselves do not expressly grant compensation for delays. However, in 2009 the Court of Justice of the EU ruled that passengers who reach their final destination three hours or more late are entitled to the same compensation as for a cancellation.

No compensation is due if the airline can prove that the disruption was caused by extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided even if all reasonable measures had been taken, such as severe weather or air-traffic-control strikes. Technical problems discovered during routine maintenance have generally not been accepted as extraordinary. Separately from compensation, airlines must provide meals, refreshments and, where necessary, hotel accommodation while passengers wait, whatever the cause of the disruption.

The rules cover all flights departing from an EU airport, and flights arriving in the EU from a non-EU country when operated by an EU airline. A revision proposed by the Commission in 2013, which would among other changes raise the delay thresholds, has been the subject of long negotiations.
statement: The delay needed for compensation has now been raised from three hours to five hours.
currentNote: Not supported. Higher delay thresholds are part of a proposed revision; the text does not say it has been adopted and gives no new figure.

The Council of the EU, where national ministers meet, is chaired by a Member State presidency that rotates every six months in an order fixed in advance. To ensure continuity, the three presidencies that follow each other work together as a 'trio' on a common 18-month programme. The presidency's role is to organise meetings, broker compromises between Member States and represent the Council in negotiations with the European Parliament; it is expected to act as a neutral broker rather than to push its own national interests. The Foreign Affairs Council is an exception: it is chaired by the High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.

The European Council, which brings together the heads of state or government, is a separate institution. It has a permanent president, elected by its members by qualified majority for a term of two and a half years, renewable once. The president chairs its meetings and represents the EU externally on foreign and security matters at that level, without prejudice to the powers of the High Representative. The European Council defines the EU's general political directions and priorities but does not exercise legislative functions.

currentNote: False. The president represents the EU on foreign and security matters 'at that level', 'without prejudice to the powers of the High Representative'.

REACH, the EU regulation on chemicals that entered into force in 2007, places the burden of proof on industry rather than on public authorities. Companies that manufacture or import a chemical substance in quantities of one tonne or more per year must register it with the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) in Helsinki, providing information on its properties, its uses and how it can be handled safely; the amount of information required increases with the quantity produced. The principle is often summarised as 'no data, no market': a substance that has not been registered cannot be manufactured or placed on the EU market in those quantities.

Substances of very high concern, such as those that cause cancer or accumulate in living organisms, can be placed on a list from which they may be moved to an authorisation list. Once that happens, they can be used only with a specific authorisation, which is granted only if the risks are adequately controlled or if the socio-economic benefits outweigh them and no suitable alternative exists. Certain uses of other substances can also be restricted across the EU.

Environmental organisations argue that identifying and restricting harmful chemicals takes too long, while industry points to the high cost of registration for small companies.
statement: Companies must register every substance they make or import under REACH, whatever the quantity.
currentNote: False. Registration applies to quantities of 'one tonne or more per year', and 'no data, no market' applies only 'in those quantities'; the text sets a threshold, so not every quantity counts.

Under an EU directive, USB-C has become the common charging port for a wide range of electronic devices. The requirement has applied to mobile phones, tablets, digital cameras, headphones, handheld video game consoles, portable speakers and similar devices since the end of December 2024, and it applies to laptops from April 2026. Devices that support fast charging must also use a common fast-charging protocol, so that any compatible charger delivers the same speed.

Consumers can also buy a new device without a charger, and packaging must show by means of a pictogram whether a charger is included, together with information about the power the device needs. The Commission expects these measures to reduce electronic waste and to save consumers money, since many households already own several compatible chargers.

Devices that are too small to have a USB-C port, such as smartwatches and some fitness trackers, are not covered. The directive also allows the Commission to update the rules as technology evolves; wireless charging, which is becoming more common, is likely to be the next area for harmonisation.
statement: Since the end of 2024, every electronic device sold in the EU has had to have a USB-C port.
currentNote: False. Many devices are covered, but small ones such as smartwatches are not, and laptops followed later.

The candidate is then elected by the Parliament by a majority of its component members; if the candidate fails to obtain that majority, the European Council must propose a new candidate within a month. currentNote: False. The text requires two-thirds 'of the votes cast', representing a majority of members, not two-thirds of all members.

The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO), based in Luxembourg, started operating in June 2021. It is an independent body responsible for investigating, prosecuting and bringing to judgment crimes against the EU's financial interests, such as fraud involving EU funds, corruption and serious cross-border VAT fraud involving damage of at least €10 million.

The EPPO was set up through 'enhanced cooperation', which means that not all Member States take part; in non-participating countries, national authorities remain responsible for these offences, and the EPPO relies on cooperation agreements with them. It works through European Delegated Prosecutors located in the participating Member States, who conduct investigations under the supervision of a central office and bring cases before national courts, applying national criminal procedure.

Before the EPPO existed, the investigation of fraud against the EU budget depended entirely on national prosecutors, whose priorities and resources varied widely, and on the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF), which can carry out administrative investigations but cannot prosecute. OLAF continues to exist, and the two bodies are expected to complement each other. In its first years, the EPPO opened investigations into estimated damages running into billions of euros.

currentNote: False. 'Not all Member States take part'; in non-participating countries 'national authorities remain responsible for these offences'.

The Treaty of Lisbon, signed in 2007, entered into force on 1 December 2009 after a difficult ratification, including a second referendum in Ireland. It largely took over the institutional reforms of the Constitutional Treaty, which had been abandoned after being rejected in referendums in France and the Netherlands in 2005, but it dropped constitutional symbols such as an official anthem and flag from the treaty text.

Lisbon made the Charter of Fundamental Rights legally binding, giving it the same legal value as the Treaties, although Poland and the United Kingdom obtained a protocol clarifying how it applied to them. It extended the ordinary legislative procedure, in which the European Parliament and the Council decide on an equal footing, to many new policy areas, and it introduced a new definition of qualified majority based on a 'double majority' of Member States and population, which took effect in 2014.

The European Council became a formal institution of the EU with a permanent president, and the post of High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy was created, combining two previous roles. The Treaty also gave national parliaments a formal role in checking that EU proposals respect the principle of subsidiarity and introduced, for the first time, a procedure allowing a Member State to leave the Union.
statement: The Treaty of Lisbon was simply the Constitutional Treaty adopted under a different name.
currentNote: False. Lisbon 'largely took over' the institutional reforms, but it dropped constitutional symbols such as the anthem and flag.

In 1965 France withdrew its representatives from most Council meetings, leaving its seat empty for about six months. The immediate dispute concerned the financing of the Common Agricultural Policy, but it was entangled with Commission proposals to give the Community its own resources and the European Parliament greater budgetary powers, and with the planned move, under the Treaty of Rome, to qualified majority voting in the Council for many decisions from 1966.

The crisis ended in January 1966 with the 'Luxembourg compromise'. The other five Member States and France recorded their agreement that, when very important national interests were at stake, the Council would try to reach a solution acceptable to all its members within a reasonable time. They also recorded their disagreement: France held that discussion should continue until unanimity was reached, while the others did not accept this. The compromise had no legal force and did not amend the Treaties.

In practice, however, it led to decisions being taken by consensus for many years, even where majority voting was possible, which many historians link to the slow pace of integration in the following decade. The Single European Act of 1986 helped restore majority voting for single-market legislation.
statement: The empty chair crisis was caused solely by a disagreement over farm financing.
currentNote: False. Farm financing was the 'immediate dispute', but it was 'entangled' with own resources, budgetary powers and majority voting.

The Working Time Directive sets minimum requirements for the organisation of working time in the EU. Workers are entitled to a minimum daily rest of 11 consecutive hours in every 24-hour period, a weekly rest period of at least 24 hours in addition to the daily rest, and at least four weeks of paid annual leave, which cannot be replaced by a payment except when the employment ends. The average working week, including overtime, must not exceed 48 hours, calculated over a reference period that is normally up to four months.

Member States may, however, allow individual workers to agree to work longer, the so-called 'opt-out', provided that the worker's consent is freely given, that no one is disadvantaged for refusing, and that employers keep records of the hours worked. Some sectors and categories, such as managing executives with autonomous decision-making powers, can be exempted from certain provisions.

The Court of Justice has interpreted the Directive broadly. It has held, for instance, that time on call spent at the workplace counts as working time even when the worker is resting, and that workers who fall ill during their annual leave are entitled to take the lost days later. Member States remain free to apply rules that are more favourable to workers.
statement: Every worker in the EU is covered by all of the Directive's limits without exception.
currentNote: False. The limits apply generally, but workers may opt out, and some categories, such as managing executives, 'can be exempted'.

When consumers buy goods online or by phone from a trader in the EU, they generally have 14 days to cancel the purchase without giving any reason. For goods, the period usually starts on the day the goods are delivered, and it remains available for twelve months after the original period ends if the trader never informs the consumer of this right. After cancelling, the consumer must return the goods, and the trader must refund all payments received, including standard delivery costs, within 14 days. The consumer may have to pay the cost of sending the goods back if the trader made this clear beforehand.

Some products are excluded from this right of withdrawal, such as goods made to the consumer's specifications, perishable items like fresh food, and sealed hygiene products that have been unsealed after delivery. Digital content such as a downloaded film can also be excluded once the download has started, provided the consumer agreed to this.

Separately from the right of withdrawal, sellers must provide a legal guarantee of at least two years, under which they must repair, replace or refund goods that turn out to be faulty. For defects that appear within the first year, it is generally presumed that they already existed at the time of delivery.
statement: Every product bought online can be returned within 14 days without giving a reason.
currentNote: False. The 14-day right is the general rule, but some products, such as perishable or made-to-order goods, 'are excluded'.

The EU Whistleblower Directive, adopted in 2019, protects people who report breaches of EU law in areas such as public procurement, financial services, product safety, environmental protection and data protection. It covers not only employees but also self-employed people, shareholders, volunteers, trainees and job applicants. Private companies with 50 or more workers, as well as public bodies, must set up internal reporting channels and acknowledge receipt of a report within seven days.

Whistleblowers may choose to report internally first or to go directly to the competent authorities. They are protected if they had reasonable grounds to believe that the information was true at the time of reporting, even if it later turns out to be inaccurate. In certain situations, for example where there is an imminent danger to the public interest or a risk of retaliation, they may also disclose the information publicly and remain protected.

Any form of retaliation, such as dismissal, demotion, intimidation or blacklisting, is prohibited, and in legal proceedings the burden of proof is reversed: the employer must show that a measure taken against the whistleblower was not linked to the report. Member States may extend protection to breaches of national law, and many have done so when transposing the Directive.

currentNote: Not supported. Acknowledgement 'within seven days' is stated, but the text sets no deadline for a full reply.

The European Accessibility Act sets common accessibility requirements for a range of products and services. Since 28 June 2025 it has applied to products such as computers, smartphones, self-service terminals like ATMs and ticket machines, and e-readers, and to services including e-commerce, banking, e-books, electronic communications and passenger transport information. The aim is to make these easier to use for persons with disabilities and older people, while giving businesses a single set of rules across the EU instead of different national requirements.

Microenterprises that provide services, defined as those with fewer than ten employees and an annual turnover or balance sheet not exceeding €2 million, are exempt from the service requirements. Any business may also claim an exemption if meeting a requirement would fundamentally alter its product or service or impose a disproportionate burden, but it must document this assessment and inform the relevant authorities.

Transition periods apply in some cases: service providers may continue to use products that they were already using before June 2025 to provide similar services until June 2030, and self-service terminals installed before that date may remain in use until the end of their economic life, but for no more than twenty years. National authorities are responsible for checking compliance and handling complaints.
statement: Since June 2025, every ATM in the EU has had to meet the new accessibility requirements.
currentNote: False. Self-service terminals 'installed before that date may remain in use until the end of their economic life', so not every ATM has had to comply since June 2025.

EU rules on food information require that the 14 most common allergens, such as gluten, nuts, milk and eggs, are highlighted in the list of ingredients, for example in bold type. For food sold without packaging, for instance in restaurants or at bakery counters, allergen information must also be available, although Member States may decide how it is provided. Most pre-packed foods must carry a nutrition declaration showing the energy value and the amounts of fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt, normally expressed per 100 g or 100 ml so that products can be compared.

Date marks come in two forms. A 'use by' date relates to safety: food should not be eaten after it, even if it looks and smells fine, and it must not be sold after that date. A 'best before' date relates to quality: after it, the food may no longer be at its best but can still be safe to eat if it has been stored correctly. The Commission estimates that confusion between the two contributes to food waste in households.

Front-of-pack nutrition labels such as the Nutri-Score are used voluntarily in several Member States, but no single scheme has been made compulsory at EU level.
statement: All foods sold in the EU must carry a nutrition declaration on their packaging.
currentNote: False. 'Most pre-packed foods' must carry a nutrition declaration, not all foods.

Since 2010, the EU organic logo, a leaf made of white stars on a green background, has been mandatory on pre-packaged organic food produced in the EU. To carry the logo, a product must contain at least 95% organic agricultural ingredients and meet strict conditions on production, processing and storage. Organic farming restricts the use of synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, prohibits genetically modified organisms and sets high animal welfare standards, including access to open-air areas.

Farms that switch to organic production must go through a conversion period, usually two years for annual crops and three years for perennial crops, during which they follow organic rules but cannot sell their products as organic. Operators are normally inspected at least once a year by control bodies, and the logo is accompanied by a code identifying the control body and an indication of where the agricultural raw materials were farmed.

The logo may also be used, voluntarily, on organic products imported from outside the EU that meet equivalent standards, and producers may add private or national organic logos next to it. currentNote: False. The logo requires 'at least 95%' organic agricultural ingredients.

Copernicus is the European Union's Earth observation programme. It relies on a family of dedicated satellites, the Sentinels, as well as on contributions from national and commercial missions and on measurements taken on the ground, at sea and in the air. Each Sentinel mission serves different needs: some carry radar instruments that can observe the surface day and night and through clouds, while others carry optical sensors similar to cameras, which need daylight and clear skies.

The data are turned into information by six thematic services covering land, the marine environment, the atmosphere, climate change, emergency management and security. The emergency service, for example, can produce maps of areas affected by floods, fires or earthquakes within hours of a request from an authorised user.

A key principle of the programme is that most of its data and information are made available free of charge and on an open basis to anyone, including businesses, researchers and the general public. Supporters argue that this policy has stimulated a market for commercial applications in areas such as agriculture and insurance, although some data, particularly for security purposes, are subject to restrictions.

currentNote: False. 'Most' data are open, but some, 'particularly for security purposes', are restricted.

The European Stability Mechanism (ESM) was set up in 2012 by the euro-area countries to help members in severe financial difficulty. Based in Luxembourg, it is an intergovernmental organisation established by a treaty between the euro-area countries rather than an EU institution, although it works closely with the European Commission and the ECB. It replaced temporary arrangements created at the height of the sovereign debt crisis.

The ESM can lend to governments and, in certain cases, help to recapitalise banks, but its assistance comes with conditions, typically a programme of economic reforms whose implementation is monitored. Major decisions, such as granting financial assistance, are taken by mutual agreement of its board of governors, made up of the euro-area finance ministers, although an emergency procedure allows decisions by a qualified majority of 85% of the votes, which are weighted according to each country's share of the capital.

The ESM raises the money it lends by issuing bonds on financial markets, backed by the capital subscribed by its members. Its loans to countries such as Greece, Cyprus and Spain carried lower interest rates and longer maturities than those countries could have obtained on the markets at the time.
statement: Every decision of the ESM's board requires the agreement of all its members.
currentNote: False. Mutual agreement is the rule for major decisions, but 'an emergency procedure allows decisions by a qualified majority of 85%', so not every decision needs all members.

Permafrost is ground that remains frozen for at least two consecutive years. It underlies around a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere, including large parts of Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada, and it contains vast amounts of organic carbon from plants and animals that died long ago, roughly twice as much as is currently in the atmosphere.

As the climate warms, permafrost is thawing, and the upper 'active layer' that thaws each summer is becoming deeper in many places. Microbes then decompose the previously frozen material, releasing carbon dioxide and methane. Whether the thawed ground releases more of one gas or the other depends largely on conditions: in waterlogged soils with little oxygen, more methane is produced. This can create a feedback loop, in which warming causes thawing that releases gases causing further warming. Scientists expect these emissions to occur gradually over decades to centuries rather than as a sudden pulse, although abrupt thaw can occur locally.

Thawing permafrost also damages buildings, roads and pipelines built on ground that was once solid. In some Arctic towns, the cost of repairing infrastructure has already risen sharply, and engineers are adapting foundations to cope with less stable ground.
statement: Permafrost thaw always happens slowly and gradually, wherever it occurs.
currentNote: False. The text says 'abrupt thaw can occur locally', which contradicts a claim that thaw is always slow wherever it occurs.

Offshore wind farms take advantage of the stronger and more consistent winds found at sea, which allow turbines to generate more electricity than comparable turbines on land. Offshore sites also allow larger turbines, since there are fewer constraints from noise and visual impact on nearby residents, and the largest models now have blades longer than a football pitch.

However, building at sea is more expensive: foundations, installation vessels, underwater cables and maintenance in harsh conditions all add to costs, and connecting distant wind farms to the grid can require major investment in transmission lines on land. Most offshore turbines stand on foundations fixed to the seabed, which limits them to relatively shallow waters; floating turbines anchored to the seabed with cables make it possible to use deeper sites, which are common off the coasts of southern Europe, but the technology is still more costly.

The North Sea has been at the centre of the industry's growth because of its shallow waters, strong winds and proximity to large electricity markets. Offshore wind farms can affect birds, marine mammals and fishing activities, so their location is usually decided through maritime spatial planning, which seeks to balance different uses of the sea.
statement: The North Sea's leading role in offshore wind is due solely to its strong winds.
currentNote: False. Strong winds are one of three reasons, alongside shallow waters and nearby markets.

Decisions under the common foreign and security policy are, as a rule, taken unanimously by the Council or the European Council, which gives each Member State a veto. The Treaty softens this rule in two ways. First, abstention does not prevent a unanimous decision, and a government may qualify its abstention with a formal declaration. This 'constructive abstention' frees it from the obligation to apply the decision, but it must accept that the decision commits the Union and refrain from any action likely to conflict with it. If the members abstaining in this way represent at least one third of the Member States comprising at least one third of the Union's population, the decision is not adopted.

Second, the Treaty lists cases in which the Council acts by qualified majority, for instance when it adopts a decision implementing a strategy already agreed unanimously by the European Council, or when it appoints a special representative. Even then, a government that declares vital and stated reasons of national policy can prevent the vote from being taken, and decisions with military or defence implications are always excluded from majority voting.

Several governments have argued for extending majority voting to more areas of foreign policy, but others, often smaller states, fear being outvoted on questions they regard as vital.
statement: Constructive abstention by states with a third of the Union's population is enough to stop a decision.
currentNote: False. A decision fails only if the abstainers are at least a third of the Member States as well as a third of the population.

Restrictive measures, commonly called sanctions, are among the Union's main foreign policy tools. They can target governments, companies, groups or individuals, and include arms embargoes, travel bans, asset freezes and restrictions on trade in particular goods. Their stated aim is not to punish but to bring about a change in policy or conduct, and they are meant to be targeted so as to limit their impact on the wider population.

Adopting them involves two steps. The Council first adopts a decision under the common foreign and security policy, which requires unanimity. Where the measures fall within the Union's competences, for instance an asset freeze or a trade restriction, the Council then adopts a regulation by qualified majority, on a joint proposal from the High Representative and the Commission. Travel bans, by contrast, are implemented by the Member States themselves. National authorities are also responsible for enforcement and for setting penalties, and a directive adopted in 2024 requires them to make intentional breaches criminal offences.

Listed persons can challenge their designation before the General Court, even though the Court of Justice otherwise has very limited jurisdiction in foreign policy. The courts have annulled a number of listings because the Council could not show sufficient evidence to support the reasons it had given.
statement: The courts annul a listing whenever the person concerned disputes the reasons given by the Council.
currentNote: Not supported. Listings were annulled where 'the Council could not show sufficient evidence', not whenever reasons are disputed.

The European Neighbourhood Policy was launched in 2004, the year of the Union's largest enlargement, to build closer relations with the countries to its east and south without offering them membership. It covers sixteen partners: ten in North Africa and the Middle East, and six in Eastern Europe and the South Caucasus, which since 2009 have also been grouped in the Eastern Partnership. Russia chose not to take part and pursued a separate relationship with the Union.

The policy offers partners closer trade ties, financial support and cooperation in areas such as energy, migration and education, in exchange for political and economic reforms. After the Arab uprisings of 2011, the Union restated this as a 'more for more' approach: partners that reform faster should receive more support. In practice, critics argue, the leverage was limited, since the most attractive incentive, a membership perspective, was not on offer, and the Union often gave priority to stability and migration control over reform.

The line between neighbourhood and enlargement has since blurred. Ukraine and Moldova were granted candidate status in 2022, and Georgia in 2023, so three eastern partners now have the membership perspective that the policy originally withheld. Belarus, by contrast, suspended its participation in the Eastern Partnership in 2021.
statement: Every eastern partner now has the membership perspective the policy originally withheld.
currentNote: False. Only three of the six eastern partners have candidate status, and Belarus has suspended its participation.

Global Gateway, presented by the European Commission in December 2021, is the European Union's strategy for investment in infrastructure in partner countries. It set out to mobilise up to €300 billion between 2021 and 2027 for projects in five areas: digital networks, climate and energy, transport, health, and education and research. It is widely seen as a European answer to China's Belt and Road Initiative, although EU officials prefer to present it as a values-based offer, stressing transparency, high environmental and social standards and the avoidance of unsustainable debt.

The headline figure needs careful reading. Only a limited part of it consists of EU grants. Much of the amount is expected to come from loans by European development finance institutions, including the European Investment Bank, and from private investors attracted by EU budget guarantees, which cover part of the risk of projects that might otherwise be considered too risky. The strategy is delivered through a 'Team Europe' approach that pools resources from the Union, its Member States and their financial institutions.

Critics argue that many projects listed under the brand were planned before 2021, and that the private capital it claims to mobilise is hard to verify. Supporters reply that the label has helped to coordinate European offers and made them more visible to partner governments.
statement: EU budget guarantees remove the risk of the projects for private investors.
currentNote: False. The guarantees 'cover part of the risk', not all of it.

passage:
Under its common security and defence policy, the European Union deploys civilian missions and military operations outside its territory for tasks such as crisis management, conflict prevention, the training of security forces and the monitoring of ceasefires. They are launched by a unanimous decision of the Council. The Union has no army of its own: personnel and equipment are provided by the Member States and, in some cases, by partner countries.

Funding follows a distinction made in the Treaty. The running costs of civilian missions are paid from the EU budget, whereas expenditure arising from operations with military or defence implications cannot be charged to it. Common costs of military operations, such as their headquarters, are therefore financed by contributions from the Member States, today through the European Peace Facility, while each country pays for the troops and equipment it sends. Most costs thus 'lie where they fall'.

The naval operation Atalanta, launched off the coast of Somalia in 2008, is one of the Union's longest-running military operations. It was set up to protect vessels of the World Food Programme and to deter piracy, and its tasks have since been widened. In 2024 the Union launched another naval operation, Aspides, to protect merchant shipping in the Red Sea; its mandate is defensive, so it does not strike targets on land.
statement: All the costs of an EU military operation lie where they fall, with the countries taking part.
currentNote: False. 'Most' costs lie where they fall; common costs such as headquarters are shared.

For centuries, questions of rank caused bitter disputes between diplomats. Envoys of rival courts quarrelled over who should enter a room first or sit nearest to a monarch, and in 1661 a clash over precedence between the retinues of the Spanish and French ambassadors in London ended in bloodshed. The Congress of Vienna addressed the problem in 1815. Its regulation divided diplomatic agents into classes and provided that, within each class, precedence would depend on the date of the official notification of an envoy's arrival, not on the prestige of the country he represented.

Many of these customs were later codified in the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961, which has been accepted by almost every state. The Convention makes the premises of a mission inviolable: officials of the host state may not enter them without the consent of the head of mission. Diplomatic agents enjoy immunity from the host state's criminal jurisdiction and, with limited exceptions, from its civil jurisdiction.

Immunity is not a licence, however. The sending state can waive it, and the host state may at any time, without giving reasons, declare a diplomat persona non grata, after which the sending state must recall the person or end his or her functions. Because expulsions are often answered by reciprocal expulsions, governments weigh them carefully.
statement: Diplomats are entirely immune from every kind of legal action brought in the host state.
currentNote: False. Civil immunity applies 'with limited exceptions', and the sending state can waive immunity.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947, cut tariffs through successive rounds of negotiations and was built on the principle of non-discrimination. Under the most-favoured-nation rule, an advantage that a member grants to goods from one trading partner must be extended immediately to similar goods from all other members. Customs unions and free trade areas are permitted as an exception, provided they cover substantially all the trade between their members.

The World Trade Organization, which replaced the GATT's institutional framework in 1995, added a stronger system for settling disputes. A panel rules first; either party may then appeal to a standing Appellate Body on questions of law; and reports are adopted unless all members agree to reject them. From December 2019, however, the Appellate Body could no longer hear new appeals, because the United States had blocked the appointment of new members. A losing party could therefore appeal a panel report 'into the void', leaving the dispute unresolved.

In response, the European Union and a number of other members set up a Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement, under which participants agree to settle appeals among themselves through arbitration. It applies only to disputes between members that have joined it.
statement: The Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement restored appeals for every dispute between members.
currentNote: False. The arrangement 'applies only to disputes between members that have joined it', so it did not restore appeals in every dispute.
